title: How to Run a Cognitive Walkthrough
intro: A structured way to catch obvious UX problems before any user touches the design. Four questions at every step, independent reviewers, no participants needed — but it's not a replacement for usability testing.

learn.title: The 4 questions at every step
learn.text:
A cognitive walkthrough simulates a brand-new user moving through a task. At every single step, each reviewer independently answers four questions:

**1. Will the user know what they're trying to do?**
Is the goal obvious at this point in the flow?

**2. Will they see the control that lets them do it?**
Is the button, link, or input visible and discoverable?

**3. Will they understand that this control does what they need?**
Does the label match their mental model?

**4. After acting, will they get feedback that it worked?**
Does the system confirm what happened?

A product demo where a PM clicks through and explains is NOT a walkthrough. If you're narrating the steps aloud, you're convincing the team the controls are discoverable — not testing if they are.

try.q: Why must reviewers work independently before discussing?
options: So each person's judgment isn't influenced by others
To save time
Because only one reviewer is needed
To make the report longer
try.explain: Independent work prevents groupthink. Mismatches between reviewers are the most valuable output — they signal likely user struggles.

learn.title: How to run it step by step
learn.text:
**1. Define a specific user goal**
Not "explore the dashboard" — something concrete like "a compliance officer generating and exporting a quarterly report for an auditor."

**2. Pick realistic entry points**
Don't default to the homepage. Real tasks start from deep links, notification emails, or alerts.

**3. Break the workflow into atomic steps**
Each step = one observable action. "Navigate to Reports" and "Click Generate" — not "Prepare compliance report."

**4. Assign independent reviewers**
Each answers the 4 questions alone. Include at least one naive reviewer from outside the product team.

**5. Compare results — mismatches are gold**
Half the reviewers thought "Generate" meant create a new report. The other half thought it meant export. That disagreement IS the finding.

**6. Validate risky steps with users**
A quick test with 3 real users confirmed "Generate" was confusing → label changed before launch.

try.q: Why should you avoid starting the walkthrough from the homepage?
options: Real tasks often start from deep links, emails, or notifications
The homepage is too simple to walk through
Users never visit the homepage
It takes too long
try.explain: Realistic entry points matter. A compliance officer doesn't start from the homepage — they click a link in a quarterly reminder email.

learn.title: When to use it (and when not to)
learn.text:
**Use walkthroughs when:**
→ Early in the project, before designs reach users
→ For complex workflows where small errors compound
→ To catch discoverability, labeling, and feedback issues
→ To avoid wasting limited participant hours on obviously broken flows

**Walkthroughs are NOT a replacement for:**
→ Usability testing with real users
→ Usage analytics after launch
→ Any method that captures actual user behavior

**Watch for confirmation bias:**
• Assuming users know what the team knows ("They'll understand 'Finalize' means submit")
• Skipping messy starting points
• Narrating steps aloud during the session

**Pro tips:**
• Rotate facilitators — don't let the PM or lead designer always run it
• Timebox each step — if you can't answer the 4 questions in a few minutes, the step is too vague
• Separate assumptions from findings — "Users will know this because..." belongs in an assumptions list

left.label: Do this
items: Validate risky steps with real users

right.label: Not this
items: Only have the product team review
Skip usability testing because the walkthrough passed

try.q: A walkthrough found no issues. Can you skip usability testing?
options: No — walkthroughs catch obvious issues but can't replace real user behavior
Yes — the walkthrough proves the design works
Only if you had 5+ reviewers
Only for simple tasks
try.explain: Walkthroughs are expert-led and catch obvious problems. But they can't simulate real user confusion, workarounds, or context — you still need usability testing.

test.q: What are the four questions asked at every step of a cognitive walkthrough?
options: Will users know the goal, see the control, understand it, and get feedback?
Is it useful, usable, desirable, and findable?
Can users learn, remember, recover from errors, and complete tasks?
Does it meet business goals, user goals, technical goals, and design goals?
test.explain: The 4 questions: (1) Know the goal, (2) See the control, (3) Understand it does what they need, (4) Get feedback after acting.

test.q: Why are mismatches between reviewers the most valuable output?
options: They signal where real users are likely to struggle too
They prove the design is fundamentally broken
They show which reviewer is wrong
They indicate the task definition was unclear
test.explain: When experienced reviewers disagree about what a control does, that's exactly where users will struggle.

test.q: Who should be included as a reviewer in a cognitive walkthrough?
options: At least one naive reviewer from outside the product team
Only senior designers
Only the PM and engineering lead
At least 5 end users
test.explain: Including someone unfamiliar with the product catches assumptions the team takes for granted.

test.q: What's wrong with a PM clicking through the prototype and explaining each step to the team?
options: Narrating the steps convinces the team controls are discoverable when they may not be
Only UX researchers are qualified to click through prototypes
PMs don't understand the design well enough
It takes too much time
test.explain: A narrated demo creates false confidence. The whole point of a walkthrough is to test if someone can figure it out WITHOUT narration.

test.q: When in the project lifecycle should you run a cognitive walkthrough?
options: Early — before designs reach users, to catch obvious issues
After launch — to confirm the design works
Only after usability testing finds problems
During the final QA sprint
test.explain: Walkthroughs belong early in the research funnel. They catch obvious issues so flawed designs don't waste limited participant hours in usability sessions.
